title: Kubernetes Advanced
description: Deepen your skills with StatefulSets, NetworkPolicy, HPA, Ingress, Jobs, storage, RBAC, and troubleshooting scenarios

questions.question: Which component is typically required to provide a stable network identity for Pods of a StatefulSet?
questions.explanation: A Headless Service (with clusterIP: None) enables direct DNS discovery of each StatefulSet Pod, giving replicas stable network identities.

questions.question: What is the typical DNS name pattern for a Pod in a StatefulSet associated with a Headless Service?
questions.explanation: StatefulSet Pods get stable DNS names of the form <pod-name>.<headless-service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, combining the Pod name and Headless Service for discovery.

questions.question: What happens when a NetworkPolicy selects Pods and defines ingress or egress rules for them?
options: All traffic in the Cluster is blocked
All traffic is allowed if there is a Service
Selected Pods are isolated in the defined direction, and only traffic matching the allowed rules is permitted
The Policy automatically changes the labels of the Pods
questions.explanation: After isolation in a given direction, only traffic allowed by the relevant NetworkPolicy rules can pass. The effect is limited to the selected Pods and direction, not the whole cluster.

questions.question: Which component typically provides the CPU and memory metrics that a standard HPA uses?
questions.explanation: Metrics Server collects and exposes resource metrics (such as CPU and memory) that Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can consume.

questions.question: Why is it important to define CPU requests when HPA is based on CPU utilization percentage?
options: Because utilization percentage is calculated relative to the Container's CPU request
To allow the Pod to receive an IP address
Because requests define the number of replicas
questions.explanation: Without an appropriate CPU request, Kubernetes cannot correctly compute utilization as a percentage of the request, so HPA targeting CPU utilization will not work reliably.

questions.question: In which API group/version is the modern stable Ingress resource defined?
questions.explanation: Stable Ingress is defined in networking.k8s.io/v1. Older APIs such as extensions/v1beta1 have been removed from modern Kubernetes versions.

questions.question: What is the difference between completions and parallelism in a Job?
options: completions is the number of Nodes and parallelism is the number of Namespaces
completions is the run time and parallelism is the DNS policy
There is no difference between them
completions is the number of required successful completions; parallelism is how many Pods can run in parallel
questions.explanation: completions defines how many successful finishes are required, while parallelism limits how many Pods may run concurrently.

questions.question: What is the default concurrencyPolicy for a CronJob?
questions.explanation: The default concurrencyPolicy is Allow, which permits Jobs created by the same CronJob to run concurrently. Forbid and Replace are alternative policies, not the default.

questions.question: Which PersistentVolume reclaim policy is considered deprecated?
questions.explanation: Recycle is deprecated and should not be relied on in new solutions. Retain and Delete remain valid reclaim policies; WaitForFirstConsumer is a binding/provisioning mode, not a reclaim policy.

questions.question: Which Access Modes are the standard recognized modes for a PersistentVolume?
questions.explanation: The classic standard Access Modes are ReadWriteOnce (RWO), ReadOnlyMany (ROX), and ReadWriteMany (RWX). ReadWriteOncePod is a newer additional mode.

questions.question: What does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer mean?
options: The PVC is deleted immediately after the Pod is created
Binding or provisioning of storage is delayed until a Pod that uses the PVC is scheduled
The Pod is forced to run on the Control Plane
questions.explanation: WaitForFirstConsumer delays volume binding/provisioning until a consuming Pod is scheduled, so topology and scheduling constraints can be considered before storage is chosen.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
options: A Role is limited to a Namespace; a ClusterRole can define cluster-scoped permissions and can also be bound with a RoleBinding in a Namespace
A Role is only for Pods and a ClusterRole is only for Nodes
A Role is for users and a ClusterRole is for passwords
questions.explanation: Role is namespaced. ClusterRole can cover cluster-scoped or namespaced resources and can be bound cluster-wide or within a Namespace via RoleBinding.

questions.question: What does apiGroups: [""] mean in an RBAC rule?
options: An empty group that grants access to no resources
The core API group, where resources such as Pods and Services live
questions.explanation: An empty string in apiGroups refers to the core API group (sometimes called the legacy group), which includes Pods, Services, and similar resources.

questions.question: Which command checks whether the user developer1 can create Pods?
options: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as developer1
questions.explanation: kubectl auth can-i checks authorization. The --as flag impersonates the requested identity so you can evaluate permissions as that user.

questions.question: What does pathType: Prefix do in an Ingress rule?
options: Exact match to the path only
Match every path for every Host
Match by path prefix, including matching path element boundaries
questions.explanation: Prefix matching uses the beginning of the path according to Kubernetes path-element boundary rules. Exact matching is pathType: Exact; HTTPS redirects are configured separately.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Service and an Ingress?
options: Both are used only for storing files
A Service is used only for CronJobs
A Service provides a stable access point to Pods; Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS routing, typically via an Ingress Controller
questions.explanation: A Service gives stable network access and load balancing to Pods. Ingress describes external HTTP/HTTPS routing rules that an Ingress Controller implements.

questions.question: What happens if a Readiness Probe keeps failing?
options: The Pod is marked not ready and typically stops receiving traffic from Services that select ready Pods
A new Deployment is created automatically
questions.explanation: Readiness determines whether the Pod should receive traffic. Repeated readiness failures remove the Pod from Service endpoints; they do not by themselves restart the container.

questions.question: What happens when a Liveness Probe fails beyond its configured failure threshold?
questions.explanation: Sustained liveness failures cause the kubelet to restart the Container. Liveness does not delete Services or create Namespaces.

questions.question: What is the difference between HPA and the Cluster Autoscaler?
options: Both only increase the number of Nodes
HPA changes the number of Nodes; Cluster Autoscaler changes the number of Pods
HPA adjusts the replica count of a workload; Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of Nodes as needed
HPA and Cluster Autoscaler are different names for the same component
questions.explanation: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales Pod replicas. Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes Nodes based on pending Pods and cluster capacity conditions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of RBAC in Kubernetes?
options: Controlling which actions an identity is allowed to perform on resources
questions.explanation: RBAC defines permissions through Roles/ClusterRoles and bindings that associate those permissions with identities.

questions.question: What is a NetworkPolicy used for?
options: Limiting ingress/egress network traffic between Pods and other destinations according to selected rules
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy defines which traffic is allowed to and from selected Pods, subject to support from the cluster's network plugin.

questions.question: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What should you check first to understand the crash cause?
options: Show the Container logs (for example with kubectl logs) and also check describe/events
Immediately change the Service to NodePort
questions.explanation: logs, logs --previous when needed, and describe/events provide information about startup errors and related events. Deleting nodes or recreating clusters is not a first diagnostic step.

questions.question: A Deployment is configured with 3 replicas, but only 2 Pods exist. Which initial check is most useful?
questions.explanation: describe shows status, events, and conditions that can explain why not all replicas were created. Also check the related ReplicaSet and Pods.

questions.question: Pods are reachable inside the Cluster, but the Service is not routing to them. What should you check first?
options: Whether the Service selector matches the Pod labels, and whether targetPort is correct
questions.explanation: A mismatched selector or incorrect targetPort are common causes. Also verify Endpoints/EndpointSlices and Pod readiness.

questions.question: How do you roll back a Deployment to a previous revision?
questions.explanation: kubectl rollout undo returns the Deployment to a previous revision in the rollout history when a suitable history entry exists.

questions.question: A Pod stays Pending and an event shows insufficient CPU. What does that mean?
options: The Scheduler could not find a Node that meets the resource and constraint requirements
The Image does not necessarily exist in the Registry
The Pod failed a Liveness Probe before it started
questions.explanation: insufficient CPU means scheduling could not place the Pod because no suitable Node had enough free CPU (or other constraints blocked placement). Image pull and liveness issues usually occur after scheduling.

questions.question: A password was stored in a ConfigMap and in a Git repository. What is the correct next step?
options: Leave it, because a ConfigMap is always encrypted
Move the secret to a Secret or appropriate secrets manager, restrict permissions, and rotate the exposed password
Move the password into a label on the Pod
Embed it in the container Image
questions.explanation: Remove the secret from unsuitable sources, rotate it because it was exposed, use Secrets or a secrets manager with proper access controls, and consider encryption at rest. ConfigMaps are not intended for sensitive data.

questions.question: You need to run a backup every day at 02:00. Which resource should you use?
questions.explanation: CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule using a cron expression, which fits a daily 02:00 backup task.

questions.question: Several Pods need to read and write the same shared files concurrently, and the storage provider supports this. Which Access Mode is appropriate?
questions.explanation: ReadWriteMany (RWX) is intended for volumes that can be mounted for read and write from multiple nodes when the CSI/backend supports it.

questions.question: You need to allow an identity to list Pods only in a specific Namespace. What is the appropriate access setup?
options: A ClusterRoleBinding with admin permissions for the entire Cluster
A Role with get/list verbs on pods and a RoleBinding in that Namespace
Add a label named read-only to every Pod
questions.explanation: A Role scopes permissions to one Namespace, and a RoleBinding associates those permissions with the identity in that Namespace. Cluster-admin is far too broad; labels and NetworkPolicy do not grant API read access.

documentation:
Kubernetes Advanced

This study guide covers advanced Kubernetes topics beyond basic Pods and Deployments: stable identities, traffic policy, autoscaling, Ingress, Jobs, storage binding, RBAC, and day-2 troubleshooting.

StatefulSets and Headless Services

StatefulSets give each replica a stable identity and ordered lifecycle. Pair them with a Headless Service (clusterIP: None) so clients can resolve individual Pods via DNS:

  • Pattern: <pod-name>.<headless-service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
  • Use when you need stable network names and often per-replica persistent storage

NetworkPolicy

NetworkPolicy selects Pods with labels and defines allowed ingress and/or egress traffic. Once a direction is constrained, only matching allowed traffic can pass. Effects apply to selected Pods, not the entire cluster, and require a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy.

Autoscaling: HPA and Cluster Autoscaler

  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): Adjusts workload replica counts from metrics such as CPU utilization.
  • Metrics Server: Common source of CPU/memory metrics for HPA.
  • CPU requests: Required for meaningful CPU utilization percentages (usage relative to request).
  • Cluster Autoscaler: Adds or removes Nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled or capacity can be reclaimed.

Ingress

  • Stable API: networking.k8s.io/v1
  • Defines HTTP/HTTPS routing to backend Services; an Ingress Controller implements the rules
  • pathType: Prefix matches by path prefix with path-element boundary rules; use Exact for full-path matches

Jobs and CronJobs

  • completions: How many successful finishes are required
  • parallelism: How many Pods may run at once
  • CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Default is Allow; alternatives include Forbid and Replace

Storage: Access Modes, Binding, and Reclaim

  • Standard Access Modes: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding/provisioning until a consuming Pod is scheduled
  • Reclaim policies: Retain and Delete are current; Recycle is deprecated

RBAC

  • Role: Namespace-scoped permissions
  • ClusterRole: Cluster-scoped (or reusable) permissions; can also be bound into a Namespace with RoleBinding
  • apiGroups: [""] means the core API group (Pods, Services, etc.)
  • Check access with kubectl auth can-i ... --as <identity>

Probes and Troubleshooting

  • Readiness Probe failure: Pod marked not ready; removed from Service traffic
  • Liveness Probe failure: kubelet restarts the Container
  • CrashLoopBackOff: Start with kubectl logs / logs --previous and describe/events
  • Missing replicas: kubectl describe deployment, then ReplicaSet and Pods
  • Service not routing: Verify selector labels, targetPort, Endpoints, and readiness
  • Pending / insufficient CPU: Scheduler found no Node meeting resource/constraint needs
  • Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
  • Secrets hygiene: Never store passwords in ConfigMaps or Git; use Secrets/secrets managers and rotate exposed credentials
